COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_dossier: Iraq sits between rival powers, competing Arab governments and an increasingly assertive Iran. Our embassies must distinguish lasting national interests from the enthusiasms of individual ministers. A coordinated foreign policy will require a diplomatic service capable of following through on Baghdad's promises.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_treaty_partner: Arms, industrial equipment and diplomatic backing are easier to secure when a powerful partner has a stake in Iraq's future. We will seek a lasting relationship with a government prepared to support our development. Such a commitment will inevitably narrow our freedom of manoeuvre.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_non_alignment: Iraq need not exchange one foreign dependence for another. By maintaining relations across the great-power divide, we can pursue our own interests and bargain with several partners. An independent course will demand more from our diplomats than the shelter of a single patron.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_partner_offer: A durable partnership must rest on more than speeches about friendship. Our representatives will approach a prospective partner with concrete proposals for cooperation and a clear account of Iraq's obligations. The agreement will stand only if both governments consider its terms worthwhile.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_multiple_offers: No single country can provide everything Iraq needs. Commercial delegations and civilian exchanges will establish contacts beyond our closest political partners. A wider network offers more opportunities, although each additional relationship requires officials who understand its particular demands.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_treaty_register: Competing ministries have too often treated foreign agreements as their own private affairs. We will bring Iraq's external commitments into a common register, allowing the government to reconcile promised assistance with actual obligations. Reliable diplomacy begins with knowing what has already been promised.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_border_settlement: The Shatt al-Arab carries both our commerce and our quarrel with Iran. Neither government can secure navigation through declarations alone. We will propose talks on the river and frontier, seeking an arrangement that protects Iraqi access while establishing terms Tehran is prepared to uphold.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_armed_deterrence: Negotiations carry little weight if our neighbours believe Iraq cannot defend its frontier. A sustained defensive posture will strengthen the forces guarding disputed approaches. The protection is valuable, but keeping trained men ready along the border will remain an expensive obligation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_border_delivery: A frontier agreement loses its value when local authorities ignore the provisions signed in the capital. Our ministries will put the agreed navigation arrangements and border guarantees into practice. The reduction of tension depends on both governments continuing to respect the settlement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_incident_channel: An isolated clash on the frontier must not leave Baghdad choosing between humiliation and an uncontrolled war. We will maintain a direct channel for examining incidents with the other government. Keeping that channel credible requires staff, records and the authority to answer quickly.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_regional_diplomacy: Iraq's ambitions cannot be sustained through public denunciations of every neighbouring government. A stronger regional diplomatic service will keep our representatives engaged in the capitals that shape Arab affairs. Influence requires a continuing presence, even where personal and ideological rivalries make cooperation difficult.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_syria: Baghdad and Damascus speak the language of Arab unity while their rival Baathist establishments compete for leadership. We will approach Syria with proposals that can be discussed on their own merits. Practical cooperation must survive the distrust between the two capitals before grander ambitions become credible.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_kuwait: Kuwait's wealth and position at the head of the Gulf make relations with it a matter of lasting Iraqi interest. Finance, navigation and the frontier each deserve serious discussion. Our delegation will seek an agreement with Kuwait's government rather than allow every dispute to become one indivisible confrontation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_party_support: Friendly movements abroad can give Iraqi diplomacy a hearing that official communiqués cannot secure. We will strengthen our contacts with compatible political organisations and improve the coordination of assistance. Sustaining these relationships demands money, experienced organisers and careful attention to the interests of the recipients.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_arab_reconciliation: Arab governments cannot confront every common problem while remaining consumed by their own quarrels. Baghdad will invite regional representatives to discuss a practical accommodation. The conference may strengthen Iraq's standing, but its conclusions will depend on what the participating governments are willing to accept.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_debt_diplomacy: Regional friendship becomes more difficult when creditors expect payment and Baghdad needs room to breathe. We will ask our partners to reconsider their financial claims in light of Iraq's circumstances. Any relief must be negotiated with those who supplied the money and now bear the risk.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_support_accounts: Political assistance abroad can disappear into overlapping organisations and promises that no ministry fully understands. A clearer account of our commitments will allow Baghdad to direct its resources where they can sustain useful relationships. Managing that network will require a permanent administrative effort.
COLDWAR_IRQ_foreign_review: Agreements that once served Iraq may become burdens as governments and regional conditions change. The Foreign Ministry will review our active commitments and prepare revisions where necessary. Replacing an obligation will require diplomacy with the other signatories, not merely a new announcement from Baghdad.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_civil_government: Dawa must turn the experience of religious opposition into the responsibilities of government. Its ministers will need to reconcile local activists, clerical counsel and a state accustomed to military command. Building a functioning administration will test the movement more severely than organising against its opponents.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_constitutional: An Islamic political programme can seek authority through a cabinet answerable to representative institutions. We will establish that relationship in law and accept the bargaining it brings. A government with a broader foundation must surrender some of the freedom enjoyed by an unchecked party leadership.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_directorial: The party's organisers argue that a divided executive would expose the new government to obstruction and renewed conspiracy. We will concentrate direction within the movement and bind the administration more closely to its programme. Greater discipline may also deepen the suspicions of those outside its ranks.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_legal_review: Religious principles must be translated into laws that courts and citizens can understand. A formal review will define the reach of religious guidance and the responsibilities of public institutions. The work requires jurists and administrators capable of resolving disputes that slogans have left unanswered.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_party_service: Local services have helped the movement establish roots where distant ministries command little trust. We will expand these networks and give their work a more dependable organisation. Their growing place in public life will bring an equally substantial burden of supervision and administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_sadr_thought: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr's writings offer a foundation for discussing faith, economic justice and political authority. The movement must decide how that intellectual guidance informs the work of its executive. Respect for religious scholarship does not settle the practical question of who directs a government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_social_justice: A government speaking in the name of Islamic justice must answer the hardship visible in Iraq's poorer neighbourhoods and villages. We will expand social provision and make support for vulnerable households a public obligation. These promises will require enduring expenditure rather than occasional charitable appeals.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_small_enterprise: Small traders, craftsmen and charitable endowments offer another foundation for social provision. We will encourage their activity and allow local initiative a larger place in the economy. Less direct state control may help enterprise grow, while leaving the treasury with a smaller share of its proceeds.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_social_accounts: Religious conviction does not excuse a government from accounting for the assistance it promises. Public welfare funds will be placed under regular financial scrutiny so that commitments can be honoured consistently. Maintaining confidence in these services requires trained officials as well as willing volunteers.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_endowment_accounts: Endowments support religious and social life, but unclear records can conceal disputes over property and responsibility. We will clarify their legal standing and bring charitable and commercial obligations into orderly accounts. Better oversight can strengthen public revenue, at the price of a larger supervisory apparatus.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_citizenship: Iraq contains communities whose confidence cannot be secured by appealing to the faith of the governing party alone. We will affirm their standing in law and their access to public institutions. A wider conception of citizenship may reassure the country while unsettling activists who demand a narrower political identity.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_najaf_schools: Najaf's institutions need not stand apart from the practical demands of a changing country. We will support technical schooling alongside religious study and give young people more routes into skilled work. Expanding the curriculum requires teachers, equipment and a continuing commitment from the state.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_independent_iraq: Shared religious commitments do not make Iraqi interests identical to those of another state. Our programme will insist that decisions concerning Iraq are taken by its own institutions. A firmer assertion of independence may strengthen the movement at home while limiting the influence available through foreign religious allies.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_trade_unions: Workers will expect the new government to hear their grievances as readily as those of religious organisations. We will recognise a framework for workplace representation and mediation. Negotiated settlements can steady the country, although production and administration must make room for the obligations they create.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_literacy: Community halls and local associations can reach adults whom the formal school system has left behind. We will equip them to teach reading and writing under a common programme. Religious service to the community should include the practical knowledge needed to deal with employers, officials and public life.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_neighbour_talks: Our neighbours must understand that an Islamic government in Baghdad speaks for Iraq. We will seek a reciprocal agreement against interference, making respect for national institutions the basis of relations. Religious affinity can open a conversation, but only an accepted agreement can give it lasting substance.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_medical_network: Illness places a heavy burden on families already struggling to make a living. A network of community medical services will bring care closer to those who cannot easily reach the larger hospitals. Maintaining clinics requires a reliable public commitment to staff, supplies and operating expenses.
COLDWAR_IRQ_dawa_government_review: The responsibilities of ministers, party organisers and religious advisers must remain clear if the cabinet is to govern effectively. We will review their respective authority and submit disputed questions to established procedures. A more secure political settlement will also place limits on the executive's discretion.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_exile_council: The council's experience in exile has given it organisation and external contacts, but governing Iraq presents different demands. Its leadership must now establish a working administration and reconcile the expectations of its supporters. Authority exercised from Baghdad must answer problems that could be postponed abroad.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_iraqi_charter: An Iraqi government needs a constitutional foundation that its citizens can recognise as their own. We will draft a charter defining the cabinet's powers and responsibilities within the country. Such limits can broaden confidence in the new order, while constraining the leadership that brought it to power.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_clerical_executive: The council's religious leadership can provide a single centre of direction in an uncertain political landscape. We will place executive authority in its hands and bind the movement more firmly to that leadership. Those excluded from this circle may see discipline as another form of imposed rule.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_representative_cabinet: A cabinet drawn only from the council's closest supporters would struggle to speak for the whole country. We will negotiate representation among Iraq's communities and political constituencies. Reaching and maintaining those arrangements will take officials, patience and a willingness to share responsibility.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_revolutionary_courts: The new authorities face demands for justice alongside pressure for immediate retribution. We will establish procedures for reviewing exceptional judgements and defining the courts' responsibilities. A more orderly legal process may restore confidence, but it cannot function without trained personnel and sustained supervision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_returnees: Families returning from exile need legal recognition, access to services and a place in communities altered by their absence. We will organise assistance and resolve their standing before disputes harden. Welcoming them home will create real demands on housing, welfare and local administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_independent_relations: Assistance received abroad must not become a permanent foreign claim on Iraqi policy. We will establish relations with Iran on the basis of decisions taken in Baghdad. This assertion of independence may reassure domestic supporters, even as it reduces the influence available through an intimate patronage relationship.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_patron_compact: The council's foreign relationships can provide support that a fragile government would struggle to obtain alone. We will formalise those connections and coordinate assistance through the movement's established networks. Relying on a patron will also expose Baghdad to expectations that cannot always be reconciled with an independent course.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_border_agreement: A government with ties to Iran still needs a settled relationship between two sovereign states. We will propose a reciprocal agreement on the frontier and political non-interference. The terms must be acceptable on both sides if cooperation is to outlast the personal connections of the council's leaders.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_aid_terms: Reconstruction assistance should strengthen the country without leaving its government uncertain of what has been promised in return. We will seek a published agreement setting out support and repayment obligations. Our prospective partners must decide whether those terms serve their interests as well as ours.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_security_state: Armed organisations cannot remain a collection of separate loyalties while claiming to defend one state. We will bring their command responsibilities and pay under a common civilian authority. More coherent forces will also require a dependable military payroll that the government must be prepared to sustain.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_southern_reconstructio: Basrah needs productive work as well as political assurances. Investment in civilian industry will give the southern economy a stronger foundation and demonstrate that the government's attention extends beyond appointments in Baghdad. The new complex must be supported by the resources of a country with many competing demands.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_religious_education: Religious institutions can remain centres of learning while preparing students for practical service to the country. We will broaden the skills taught alongside religious scholarship and support the staff needed to do so. The government must provide a lasting educational commitment if this ambition is to endure.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_minority_charter: Communities outside the council's principal constituency have good reason to examine the character of its rule. A charter will affirm their legal protections and place duties upon public authorities. Securing their confidence may require the movement to temper demands from its more exclusive supporters.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_water_services: Dependable water and local services are among the most direct tests of government in the south. We will invest in the infrastructure needed to support them and improve everyday conditions. Religious and political authority will carry more weight when residents can see practical attention to their needs.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_school_access: A child's access to schooling should not depend on a family's standing within the governing movement. We will extend teaching to communities poorly served by existing institutions. Opening those classrooms can give the new government a broader foundation than the networks that sustained it in exile.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_civil_review: Extraordinary authority may help a movement take power, but it creates disputes once ordinary government must resume. We will review emergency powers and the responsibilities of civilian institutions. Placing firmer limits on the executive can steady the country while making unilateral decisions more difficult.
COLDWAR_IRQ_sciri_iraqi_mandate: The council cannot govern indefinitely on the strength of its record abroad. Its leaders must secure a domestic mandate and accept obligations toward citizens beyond their own organisation. Establishing that settlement will strengthen public confidence at the expense of some of the leadership's freedom of action.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_return: The Iraqi Islamic Party must rebuild an open political organisation after years in which its activity depended on restricted and underground networks. A renewed leadership will bring those circles together and define their responsibilities. Moving into public government demands more than the habits that preserved the movement under pressure.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_parliamentary: The party can advance its religious and social programme through a cabinet answerable to representative institutions. We will accept contested politics and the need to negotiate with other forces. That choice offers a broader foundation for government while placing real limits on the leadership's authority.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_directorial: Party organisers argue that a strong central executive is necessary to protect the movement and carry out its programme. We will make their organisation the principal channel of political direction. Greater internal discipline may also increase resistance among those unwilling to accept a party-directed state.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_law: Religious commitments must be expressed in rules that public institutions can administer consistently. We will define legal rights, obligations and the limits of official authority. Turning a political programme into dependable law will require jurists and civil servants with the capacity to enforce it.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_associations: Associations rooted in neighbourhoods, congregations and professions can sustain the party beyond the capital. We will strengthen their organisation and connect them more closely to the movement's leadership. A dependable national network needs offices and experienced organisers whose work cannot rest on enthusiasm alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_civil_service: A conservative cabinet still needs engineers, accountants and administrators capable of running a modern state. We will give professional qualifications greater weight in appointments and allow specialists to direct their own work. Party leaders must accept some loss of immediate control if competence is to mean anything.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_social_market: Private enterprise has an important place in the party's vision of a moral economy. We will encourage traders and manufacturers to expand their activity under clear commercial rules. Giving them greater freedom can improve production, although the state will retain less direct command over the revenue it creates.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_welfare: A conservative government cannot leave social hardship entirely to families and voluntary generosity. We will establish a more dependable welfare commitment for households that need assistance. The cohesion it brings will depend on the treasury continuing to meet obligations that political speeches alone cannot fulfil.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_business_law: Small firms cannot plan confidently when contracts depend on personal connections and uncertain enforcement. We will strengthen commercial law and extend its reach beyond the capital. More predictable business relations can support investment, provided the state maintains the officials and courts required to uphold them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_charity_accounts: Charitable organisations command local trust, but their work must be coordinated with the government's own responsibilities. We will clarify their accounts and the public commitments they help to meet. Honest supervision can protect confidence in the system while adding to the duties of the administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_national_compact: The government must offer security to citizens who do not share the party's religious or political outlook. We will affirm a common legal standing for Iraq's communities and their access to public institutions. Such a compact requires a broader national language than some within the movement would prefer.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_education: Local associations can help bring reading and writing to adults who have had little contact with formal schooling. We will support community education and provide the materials needed for regular teaching. A better educated public will be more capable of taking part in economic and civic life.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_foreign_policy: Relations abroad should serve the government's conception of Iraqi interests while maintaining useful ties with sympathetic states. We will give those relationships sustained diplomatic attention. Close political affinities can open doors, although they may also make it harder to present Baghdad as an entirely independent voice.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_labour_compromise: Industrial peace requires an arrangement that employers and workers can both recognise. The government will support mediation and a common framework for workplace disputes. A more stable relationship will place demands on administrators and sometimes oblige factories to accommodate claims they would otherwise dismiss.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_public_service: Public employment should reward the ability to perform a job rather than access to the party's inner circles. Service examinations will give qualified applicants a clearer route into the administration. Improving the state's competence means asking political leaders to surrender part of their patronage.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_arab_offer: Arab cooperation can offer Iraq useful commercial and educational links without requiring every partner to adopt the same political programme. We will approach a prospective partner with proposals for civilian exchange. Their value will depend on both governments being willing to sustain the relationship.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_medical_welfare: The party's social commitments must be visible in the care available to ordinary families. We will support community medical and welfare services where existing provision is weak. A dependable system requires regular expenditure on trained staff and supplies, rather than reliance on occasional donations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iip_government_mandate: A governing movement must renew its claim to authority through the institutions it has chosen for the country. We will settle the procedures for leadership and public responsibility within that framework. A durable mandate can strengthen confidence, but it also binds the cabinet to rules beyond its own convenience.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_accounts: Iraq's petroleum wealth means little if the government cannot establish what the concessions produce and what the treasury receives. We will examine export accounts and contractual payments in detail. A stronger claim to the country's oil revenues begins with officials able to follow the money.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_nationalize: The Iraq Petroleum Company's position leaves a foreign concessionary structure at the heart of our economy. We will take control of its operations and assert the state's authority over petroleum development. Sovereignty will bring responsibility for management, technical continuity and the external consequences of this decision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_renegotiate: The existing concessions can be challenged without ending foreign technical participation altogether. We will demand revised terms that give Iraq a greater share of its petroleum wealth. Keeping cooperation alive will depend on reaching an agreement that the other parties are prepared to honour.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_state_company: National control must be exercised by an organisation that can keep the fields working and the accounts in order. We will build a national oil service with its own engineers, managers and commercial staff. A functioning company can ease the transition, but its responsibilities will remain substantial.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_concession_delivery: Revised concession terms must reach the export accounts and the government's receipts before they can change Iraq's position. We will put the accepted agreement into operation and supervise its obligations. The new arrangement preserves technical cooperation while leaving a continuing foreign stake in the industry.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_technical_training: Dependence on imported expertise limits how confidently Iraq can direct its own oil industry. We will train engineers able to operate equipment, evaluate new methods and supervise technical work. Building that knowledge within the country will also strengthen the skills available to other industries.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_revenue_state: Petroleum exports offer the quickest route to financing the government's ambitions. We will organise development around that income and give the export sector priority. A state that leans so heavily on oil has less reason to cultivate the wider tax base on which a more varied economy would depend.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_diversification: An economy built around the next tanker shipment remains exposed to decisions made far beyond Iraq. We will direct more resources toward construction and production outside the petroleum sector. The effort asks the country to forgo some immediate export income in exchange for a broader economic foundation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_export_terminals: Oil revenues depend on the ability to move exports through the south as well as on production in the fields. We will improve Basrah's transport infrastructure and the connections serving export handling. Better links will help turn petroleum output into a more dependable commercial flow.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_industrial_fund: Oil income can finance productive capacity that survives fluctuations in the petroleum market. We will support a new civilian industrial complex and give development outside the fields a firmer base. The country's underground wealth should leave something more durable than a succession of government expenditures.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_revenue_ledger: Separate accounts and conflicting reports make it difficult to judge Iraq's position in the oil market. We will reconcile export receipts and commercial obligations in a common record. Clearer information will reduce duplicated work and allow ministers to respond more coherently to changing conditions abroad.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_kirkuk_survey: Kirkuk remains central to Iraq's petroleum economy, yet its further development requires sound knowledge of the producing area. We will finance a detailed survey and prepare the resources it identifies for use. The work should be guided by what the field can sustain, rather than ministerial expectations alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_baiji: Crude production must be matched by the ability to process fuel for the country's needs. We will improve refining work at Baiji and strengthen the organisation supporting it. More effective processing will require an administrative system capable of keeping equipment, staff and supplies working together.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_reserve_policy: Selling every available shipment leaves little protection when domestic fuel demand rises or supplies are interrupted. We will give petroleum reserves a more deliberate place in national planning. Holding resources for security will mean accepting less immediate income from exports.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_field_maintenance: A producing field can lose much of its value through neglected equipment and poorly organised maintenance. We will strengthen inspections, repairs and the supply of essential parts. On the nationalised course, reliable field management will complete the difficult transition to operating without the old concessionary administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_operators: New installations are of limited use without operators who understand the machinery entrusted to them. We will expand practical instruction for refinery and maintenance personnel. A stronger technical workforce will help the industry absorb improved methods and make more effective use of its equipment.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_contract_review: Export contracts must remain suitable for the market in which Iraqi oil is actually sold. Our commercial representatives will review the terms as agreements come up for renewal. Baghdad can press for better conditions, but buyers and partners must still be persuaded to sign them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_oil_sovereignty: Control of petroleum wealth is secured through dependable receipts as much as through declarations of ownership. We will strengthen the accounts through which oil income reaches the state and ensure that obligations are recorded clearly. Maintaining sovereign control requires officials capable of exercising it every day.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_survey: Plans for industrial growth must reckon with the power, land and skilled labour actually available to Iraq. We will survey existing capacity and establish a more orderly programme of investment. The resulting commitments will need continued attention from officials who can distinguish a viable project from an impressive promise.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_heavy: A stronger industrial base requires large plants and the capacity to sustain demanding production. We will concentrate investment on heavy industry and develop factories capable of more efficient work. Such concentration will draw resources away from the everyday needs of consumers.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_light: Households and civilian businesses need more of the goods that an oil-dependent economy too readily imports. We will give light industry a larger place in development and help manufacturers improve their methods. This choice leaves fewer resources available for expanding military production.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_steel: Baghdad's industrial districts can support a wider network of workshops and civilian manufacturers. We will establish a new industrial complex to give that expansion a physical foundation. Productive investment in the capital must turn plans and imported machinery into regular work for Iraqi industry.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_consumers: Provincial workshops cannot meet the growing demand for clothing, household goods and everyday supplies. A new industrial complex in Nineveh will give local manufacturers room to expand and reduce the concentration of production around Baghdad. Provincial development must become a practical part of our industrial policy.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_power_grid: Factories cannot work reliably when the connections supporting them lag behind the machinery inside their walls. We will strengthen industrial infrastructure and the links that keep production moving. New investment must be accompanied by the administrative capacity to maintain it once construction has finished.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_public_finance: Development financed from public resources gives Baghdad a clearer claim over the direction of investment. We will strengthen revenue collection and devote more of the country's means to state projects. The effort will place additional demands on households and the civilian economy supporting those ambitions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_credit_finance: Foreign credit can bring industrial projects forward before the treasury could finance them unaided. We will seek a development loan with terms the government can defend and repay. Access to another country's capital must be negotiated with a lender willing to accept the risk.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_public_accounts: An industrial appropriation does not guarantee that machinery arrives or a factory works as intended. Inspectors and better accounts will follow public investment from expenditure to productive use. More effective supervision can help industry improve, provided the government maintains the staff required to carry it out.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_debt_accounts: Borrowed money has helped finance development, but repayments must not be left to compete blindly with every new ambition. We will establish a more orderly approach to servicing industrial credit. Keeping faith with creditors will require actual resources from a treasury already supporting the country's other programmes.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_maintenance: A factory that waits indefinitely for a replacement part is an expensive monument to poor planning. We will organise maintenance, technical staffing and the supply of spares across the industrial sector. Keeping existing plants productive requires a continuing administrative effort alongside the enthusiasm for new construction.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_power: Industrial growth and expanding towns are placing greater demands on the southern power supply. A thermal power project in Basrah will provide a stronger foundation for that development. Electricity production must become a dependable part of national investment rather than an afterthought to each new factory.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_machine_tools: The quality of tools and the skill of those using them determine what Iraqi workshops can achieve. We will expand technical instruction and improve familiarity with modern production methods. A stronger command of machine tools will help existing factories reach standards that new buildings alone cannot provide.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_commercial_services: Manufacturing needs offices that can arrange sales, keep accounts and coordinate the movement of goods. We will expand commercial services in Baghdad to support the country's growing economy. A stronger business infrastructure will give productive enterprises more reliable connections to customers, suppliers and finance.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_grid_management: More generating capacity will accomplish little if power and industrial connections are poorly coordinated. We will strengthen the administration responsible for dispatch and infrastructure planning. Better coordination can support construction across the country, although the service itself will require a dependable operating budget.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_quality: Factories under pressure to meet targets can produce goods that fail long before they should. We will introduce more systematic inspection and help managers correct faults in production. Better standards will take time and resources that cannot be devoted immediately to increasing output.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_tax_service: Industrial expansion should support public revenue rather than disappear behind incomplete registers and informal arrangements. We will improve tax records and the officials responsible for maintaining them. A more capable service can collect what is owed, but competent administration carries its own continuing expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_industry_delivery_review: The next round of investment should reflect what earlier projects have taught us. Ministers will review the balance between industrial priorities and redirect future commitments where necessary. A credible development programme must be willing to change course without abandoning the productive assets already built.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_land_survey: Changing ownership on paper has not resolved the shortage of credit, equipment and dependable water in the countryside. We will examine how the land reform operates in practice and identify the obstacles facing cultivators. An honest survey will require officials willing to look beyond favourable reports from provincial authorities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_cooperatives: Small cultivators often cannot obtain machinery and services on their own. Farm cooperatives will pool those needs and make agricultural support easier to organise at scale. The promise of stronger production will depend on an administration capable of assisting the associations without simply overwhelming them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_smallholders: Independent cultivators need the confidence and means to improve the land they work. We will support smallholders through practical assistance and more favourable access to credit. Leaving them a greater share of their resources can strengthen production while reducing what the state immediately collects from rural activity.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_cooperative_credit: Cooperatives cannot fulfil their purpose if they exist without the machinery and advice needed in the fields. We will support equipment purchases and organise assistance around their members' requirements. Delivering these services will begin to close the gap between agrarian reform and everyday agricultural work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_smallholder_credit: A smallholder without access to credit remains dependent on poor tools and uncertain harvests. We will guarantee a more useful flow of finance to independent producers and help them improve their farms. The state must accept a financial sacrifice if land reform is to produce viable livelihoods.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_water_accounts: Water administration cannot remain a collection of local demands with no clear national picture. We will improve records and coordinate the authorities responsible for irrigation along the two rivers. More informed allocation can help production, provided the government sustains the field administration needed to make it work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_large_irrigation: Large irrigation works offer the prospect of serving broad agricultural areas under a common plan. We will concentrate resources on a central programme of improvement. Its scale can strengthen production, but it will also absorb means that might otherwise support the immediate demands of civilian life.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_local_irrigation: Many farming communities need improvements suited to their own channels and fields rather than a distant grand scheme. We will support local irrigation works and give field authorities a larger role. A dispersed programme can reach practical needs, although it requires more sustained local supervision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_wasit: Wasit's cultivators need investment that reaches the productive land rather than ending in the offices of a ministry. We will develop an agricultural district and strengthen the foundation for local farming. The countryside must see tangible results from the government's promises of rural development.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_dhiqar: Agricultural development in Dhi Qar must address the practical requirements of communities far from the capital. We will establish a new agricultural district and support a stronger productive base in the province. Investment in the south should give rural households more reason to remain on the land.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_extension: Credit and machinery are less effective when cultivators have nowhere to turn for reliable technical advice. A rural extension service will bring agricultural specialists into regular contact with the people working the fields. Their work can resolve persistent weaknesses, provided the state supports the service beyond its initial announcement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_grain_storage: A harvest loses value when poor roads and unreliable handling prevent it from reaching storage and markets. We will improve the transport connections serving agricultural communities in Qadisiyah. Better rural links will help the work already done in the fields translate into a more dependable food supply.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_river_talks: Iraq's farmers depend on rivers whose courses begin beyond our frontiers. We will invite the upstream governments to discuss a more predictable approach to water management. Domestic investment remains essential, but lasting arrangements on shared rivers require neighbours prepared to make and respect reciprocal commitments.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_marsh_livelihoods: The marsh communities rely on ways of working that distant ministries too easily overlook. We will support local livelihoods and the services needed to sustain them. Rural production can be strengthened by working with these communities, although adequate provision will add to the government's continuing social obligations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_distribution: Rural hardship is worsened when produce cannot reach consumers efficiently and supplies reach villages only at excessive cost. We will improve the organisation of agricultural distribution. A more dependable network can ease the burden on households, but it will require regular coordination and supervision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_water_inspection: Canals and irrigation works can deteriorate long before their failures appear in an annual report. We will strengthen field inspection and give the responsible authorities better knowledge of local conditions. Maintaining useful agricultural infrastructure requires staff who can identify problems and follow repairs through to completion.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_clinics: Distance from a hospital should not leave rural families without basic medical care. Mobile clinics will bring trained staff and essential services to communities the permanent network serves poorly. The confidence this can build depends on meeting the continuing cost of reaching scattered settlements.
COLDWAR_IRQ_agri_reform_delivery: Agrarian reform will be judged by the farms and households it leaves behind, not the decrees that began it. We will consolidate the rural credit, advice and distribution services now reaching the countryside. A more workable settlement requires continued administration, but can finally overcome the weaknesses left by an unfinished reform.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_baseline: The ambition to modernise Iraq rests on a population still unevenly served by schools and public institutions. We will establish a clearer picture of literacy, skills and access to essential services. National policy must begin with the people whom existing provision has failed to reach.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_mass_literacy: A great many adults have been denied the schooling needed to read public notices, keep accounts or pursue skilled work. We will organise a broad literacy campaign and carry teaching beyond the ordinary classroom. The country's development must draw on people who have too long remained outside formal education.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_teacher_first: An expanding education system needs teachers who can do more than repeat lessons from a scarce textbook. We will invest first in their preparation and the skills that sustain effective instruction. Building that foundation will require a continuing social commitment before its full value becomes apparent.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_evening_classes: Work and family responsibilities prevent many adults from attending ordinary lessons. Evening classes will give them another opportunity to learn reading and writing without abandoning their livelihoods. A regular programme in accessible local buildings can extend education to people a conventional school timetable leaves behind.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_teacher_deployment: Training teachers is only part of the task; they must reach the places that need them. We will organise their deployment and provide the support required to keep classrooms operating. Better prepared instruction should become a lived improvement in the towns and villages still poorly served.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_literacy_accounts: Campaign reports are useful only if they describe what people have actually learned. We will improve the assessment of literacy and make educational authorities answer for the results of their work. Careful records can guide future teaching, although maintaining them adds to the duties of the administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_universal_services: Public services should offer every Iraqi a recognised claim on the state, rather than depend on place, influence or personal need. We will establish a broad commitment to provision across the country. The confidence it creates must be matched by a budget capable of sustaining an extensive system.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_targeted_services: The treasury cannot answer every unmet need at once. We will concentrate assistance on the households and districts where a more limited programme can make the greatest difference. This approach restrains the overall commitment, but demands officials capable of deciding who qualifies and defending those decisions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_primary_care: Larger hospitals cannot meet the everyday needs of a country whose communities are widely scattered. We will strengthen provincial primary care and bring routine treatment closer to home. Better access can build public confidence, provided clinics receive a dependable share of staff, supplies and operating funds.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_priority_districts: Some districts have received little from national development beyond promises made in the capital. We will direct assistance toward neglected communities and establish a clearer basis for selecting them. Fairer provision requires administrators able to resist the pressure of influential constituencies seeking preferential treatment.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_budget_review: Education and welfare promises must be reconciled with the revenue available to honour them. We will review public commitments and strengthen the administration supporting the social budget. More dependable accounts can help the state sustain its services, but they require trained officials and continuing supervision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_women_education: Iraq cannot develop its full range of skills while so many women lack access to education. We will support teaching and professional preparation that opens more opportunities to them. Giving these ambitions practical substance requires classrooms, instructors and a willingness to reach beyond established patterns of opportunity.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_housing: Growing towns need more than additional rooms behind crowded walls. We will invest in the infrastructure supporting housing and urban services so that expanding neighbourhoods can function properly. Municipal development must keep pace with the people seeking work and a better life in the cities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_technical_colleges: Industry and public services need technicians whose preparation goes beyond basic schooling. We will support colleges able to teach practical subjects and develop a stronger body of specialist knowledge. The benefit to national development will depend on a lasting commitment to instructors, equipment and institutional support.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_rural_schooling: Children and adults in the countryside should not have to leave their communities to gain basic education. We will extend teaching to rural areas and support the work needed to keep it available. Development will remain uneven if access to reading and writing continues to follow the boundaries of the towns.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_municipal_finance: Local authorities cannot maintain services on uncertain grants and incomplete revenue records. We will improve collection and give municipalities a more dependable financial administration. A stronger local tax base can support growing settlements, although administering it requires staff and resources of its own.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_science_maintenance: Laboratories lose their value when instruments break, materials run short or trained staff depart. We will provide more reliable support for civilian scientific work and the facilities on which it depends. Research capacity must be maintained patiently if it is to serve the country's wider development.
COLDWAR_IRQ_society_service_compact: The public service programme must be able to adapt as needs and resources change. We will review the balance of coverage and funding while preserving the educational progress already achieved. A more durable settlement should rest on commitments the government can continue to meet.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_accounts: The armed forces need a clear account of their institutions, expenditure and readiness. We will examine how resources move through the military administration and identify the obstacles facing the forces already under arms. A stronger defence policy begins with knowing what the state is actually supporting.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_professional: A dependable army needs a trained core capable of holding formations together under pressure. We will give professional service and unit cohesion greater weight in military development. Retaining capable personnel will require a more substantial payroll than a system built around brief service and rapid turnover.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_mass: Iraq must be able to draw on a wider body of reservists when its security is threatened. We will organise a broader reserve army and expand the pool available for service. Mobilising more men will place strain on cohesion and the standards that a smaller professional force can maintain.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_staff_training: Orders lose their value when headquarters cannot coordinate the forces expected to carry them out. We will strengthen staff instruction and give officers more demanding preparation for command. A more capable army will have to devote additional time to training before its formations are ready.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_reserve_training: Names on a reserve register are no substitute for men who remember their duties and can rejoin a functioning formation. We will establish a more dependable training programme for the reserves. Maintaining that preparation will add to the military's continuing personnel commitments.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_procurement_board: Separate purchasing arrangements leave the armed forces with conflicting requirements and poorly coordinated maintenance. A procurement board will bring suppliers, production needs and support contracts into a common process. More effective acquisition requires a military administration able to follow each commitment through.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_soviet_standard: A common body of Soviet equipment and support practices can simplify the burden on our military supply system. We will align procurement and servicing around that standard. Greater consistency will make the forces easier to sustain, while increasing reliance on a supplier whose interests remain its own.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_mixed_supply: Dependence on one source exposes the armed forces to decisions made abroad. We will maintain a wider range of suppliers and strengthen the capacity to absorb their equipment. The additional choice will come with a more complicated burden of parts, manuals and incompatible servicing requirements.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_soviet_offer: A foreign advisory mission can help our officers make better use of the equipment and methods already available to them. We will approach the Soviet government with a proposal for assistance. The mission's role and obligations must be agreed before advisers can contribute to the army's development.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_maintenance_manuals: An inventory assembled from different sources needs maintenance instructions that workshops can actually use. We will reconcile technical documentation and organise the support required to keep equipment serviceable. Better methods can strengthen production and repair, provided the administration sustains the work behind them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_logistics: Units cannot remain effective when their supplies are directed through competing offices. We will strengthen a unified logistics administration and improve coordination between depots and formations. A more economical supply system will depend on trained staff and a continuing budget for its operation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_land_schools: The army needs institutions that teach practical soldiering and prepare men to restore cohesion after disruption. We will support training schools serving the existing forces. Their contribution will be measured in more dependable units, but it also entails a lasting commitment to instructors and military personnel.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_air_maintenance: Aircraft depend on technical institutions as much as on the men in the cockpit. We will improve the training and organisation of air maintenance personnel and strengthen their command of engineering practice. Sustaining that knowledge requires administrative support beyond the purchase of new machines.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_coastal: Iraq's short coastline deserves a practical maritime support base suited to its circumstances. We will develop dockyard capacity in Basrah and strengthen the foundations of coastal defence. A modest industrial foothold will serve the fleet more usefully than ambitions unsupported by facilities ashore.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_armaments: An army dependent on foreign deliveries benefits from a stronger domestic base for military production. We will establish an armaments factory in Salahuddin and give national industry a larger role in sustaining the forces. The new capacity must become part of a workable supply system.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_fuel_discipline: Careless movement, poor servicing and wasteful operating practices consume fuel the army may need urgently elsewhere. We will make fuel discipline a regular part of military administration and training. More economical operations require officers and specialists who can monitor use without leaving formations unprepared.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_ship_maintenance: A coastal fleet needs skilled dockyard workers who can keep vessels in service rather than wait for help from abroad. We will strengthen maritime maintenance and the organisation behind it. Better dockyard work requires an institutional commitment appropriate to the facilities on which the fleet depends.
COLDWAR_IRQ_defence_readiness: Readiness cannot be sustained indefinitely through inspection reports and orders to work harder. We will establish organised periods of intensive preparation with the resources to support them. The government must choose when the additional personnel commitment is worth carrying and allow the forces time between such efforts.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_contingency: A government that waits for a crisis to organise itself has already surrendered valuable choices. We will prepare contingency plans linking military requirements with civilian administration. The work demands officials and coordination even while Iraq remains at peace and hopes never to need the plans.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_restraint: Iraq can defend its interests without treating every confrontation as the opening of an offensive campaign. We will sustain a credible defensive posture while leaving room for diplomacy. Keeping that restraint convincing requires forces whose readiness must still be paid for.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_offensive_option: There are disputes in which Baghdad may judge that pressure must rest on the possibility of attack. We will prepare the army for that course and develop a more assertive military posture. The cost begins before fighting, in higher personnel commitments and greater anxiety over the government's intentions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_crisis_channel: A confrontation can narrow the government's choices faster than either side intends. We will maintain diplomatic channels and seek mediation where an outside government can carry a useful proposal. Preserving room for negotiation requires people with the authority and resources to keep talking during a crisis.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_deliberate_authority: Preparing for war and choosing to begin one are different responsibilities. We will establish a clear process for authorising a specific military proposal and examining the interests it is meant to serve. Such a decision must belong to the government rather than emerge from an unchecked chain of preparations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_civil_continuity: The public administration must keep functioning when military preparations dominate the attention of ministers. We will organise civil authority to maintain essential government work through a crisis. That continuity requires planning, staff and clear responsibilities before events place the whole state under pressure.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_economy: Fighting requires a flow of replacements that ordinary production priorities may not provide. We will direct more of the economy toward military output and expand the resources supporting the army. The burden will be felt in civilian consumption and the growing cost of keeping men under arms.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_civilian_floor: The civilian population cannot be treated as an inexhaustible reserve for military expenditure. We will protect a minimum commitment to public services and everyday needs. Holding that line can sustain confidence at home, but it will restrict the output available to the war effort.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_procurement_cycle: Wartime orders must reach factories in a form that suppliers can carry out. We will coordinate military procurement more closely and help production respond to the army's changing demands. The gains depend on an administrative effort maintained for the duration of the emergency.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_services_continuity: War does not suspend illness, schooling or the obligations of the state toward its citizens. We will sustain essential civilian services despite the claims of the front. Preserving those institutions can steady the country, provided the government continues to meet their costs.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_accounts: An emergency invites commitments that no ministry expects another to question. We will strengthen the accounts covering public revenue and extraordinary expenditure before disorder becomes permanent. More dependable collection and supervision will require officials able to follow military as well as civilian obligations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_veterans: Those returning from war, and the families bearing its losses, will expect more than public ceremony. We will establish support for veterans and victims as a lasting responsibility of government. Meeting that duty can strengthen the country, but the social cost will remain after the guns fall silent.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_reconstruction: War has left civilian capacity damaged or lost while communities still depend on it for work and daily necessities. We will direct reconstruction toward those actual losses and restore a productive foundation. Recovery must make good the destruction before the country can resume its wider ambitions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_credit_burden: The money that sustained the country through war now limits what its government can afford in peace. We will approach creditors and seek a settlement of the burden. Their willingness to compromise will depend on their own interests as well as Baghdad's account of what the fighting achieved.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_reintegration: The end of fighting leaves people and institutions organised around an emergency that has passed. We will support the transition back to civilian life and review the obligations created by mobilisation. A steadier settlement requires social expenditure even as the government seeks relief from wartime demands.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_recovery_contracts: Reconstruction needs firms and workshops capable of restoring useful production, rather than simply securing the next public contract. We will organise recovery work around the capacity the country has lost. Better supervision can improve results, although it adds to the administration supporting the rebuilding effort.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_sanctions_response: Restrictions imposed from abroad threaten the country's ability to recover and meet its obligations. We will seek a diplomatic review and examine what terms might reopen useful relations. Relief depends on persuading the governments maintaining the sanctions that a change serves their interests.
COLDWAR_IRQ_war_peace_dividend: A country cannot remain indefinitely organised for the next emergency. We will review exceptional commitments and place greater weight on the security that comes from a sustainable civilian settlement. A less costly military posture can support that course while the state continues to meet its lasting obligations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_frontier: The quarrel over the Shatt al-Arab has brought the imbalance between Iraq and Iran into sharp relief. Baghdad must decide how to confront a powerful neighbour while its own institutions remain strained. A deliberate assessment of the eastern frontier will give ambition a firmer foundation than angry declarations alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_shatt_demand: Control of the river remains a question of prestige as well as navigation. We will renew Baghdad's demand for the Shatt al-Arab and make clear that the frontier dispute cannot be ignored. A more forceful claim may rally supporters, but it also raises the prospect of a confrontation the country must carry.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_arabistan_claim: Nationalists look across the frontier to Khuzestan and speak of Arabistan as part of Iraq's rightful regional inheritance. We will place that claim at the centre of a more ambitious eastern policy. Its oil, ports and strategic position are a powerful prize, but a public demand will not secure the province's allegiance.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_southern_command: A campaign in the south would demand more than moving formations toward the border. We will strengthen the command responsible for the theatre and prepare officers for coordinated operations and river crossings. A force capable of attempting such a campaign will require a larger continuing personnel commitment.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_tehran_assessment: Our plans must be grounded in the condition of Iran's army rather than confidence in its supposed weakness. Intelligence officers will assess its command, cohesion and capacity to respond. If serious disorder presents an opening, Baghdad should be ready to recognise it without building its entire strategy on an assumption.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_operational_plan: An advance into Khuzestan will succeed only if command arrangements and supply planning match the army's ambitions. We will bring reconnaissance and southern preparations into a coherent operational plan. Better coordination can reduce waste, but the headquarters supporting it will need experienced staff and sustained resources.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_short_war: A concentrated opening blow could seize the initiative before Iran brings its strength to bear. We will prepare for a rapid advance into Khuzestan and seek a decision through the first campaign. The opportunity will be brief; a stalled offensive could leave Iraq committed to a very different war.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_sustained_war: Iran may absorb an initial setback without abandoning the struggle. We will prepare the industrial and personnel foundations for a longer campaign instead of staking everything on a sudden collapse. Sustaining that effort will draw skilled people and resources away from civilian development and research.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_fuel_spares: A formation that runs short of fuel or essential parts can lose the initiative without meeting the enemy. We will organise reserves and maintenance support for the projected campaign. More disciplined operations can make supplies go further, provided the army maintains the administration needed to keep them moving.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_mobilisation_base: A sustained campaign needs an industrial base capable of replacing what the army consumes. We will establish additional military production in Salahuddin and support the personnel required for mobilisation. The commitment gives our plans greater substance while adding to the cost of keeping a larger war effort ready.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_gulf_credit: Other Gulf governments may see Iran's power as a danger they would rather Iraq confront. We will seek financial backing and present our preparations as serving a wider regional interest. Assistance can strengthen our position, but money advanced in solidarity may later return as a creditor's demand.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_forward_depots: An offensive cannot be supplied entirely from distant stores once the army crosses difficult ground. We will organise forward depots and improve the movement of supplies toward the southern front. The logistical advantage will depend on a larger support apparatus working before and during the campaign.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_war_contracts: Factories must know what the army will need before losses force hurried purchases. We will arrange production contracts to support replacement and sustain the campaign's material demands. Giving military supply a more dependable place will come at the expense of revenue and civilian priorities elsewhere.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_supplier_access: Foreign equipment remains useful only while the army can obtain the parts and support needed to keep it working. We will approach suppliers about arrangements suitable for a wartime demand. Baghdad must secure their cooperation on terms they accept rather than assume that earlier sales guarantee assistance.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_final_ultimatum: Preparation has brought Baghdad to a decision that further declarations cannot postpone. We will present Iran with our demand for Khuzestan and establish the basis for enforcing it. Tehran may refuse; the government must then judge whether the strategic prize justifies committing the country to war.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_launch_campaign: The southern plan must now be ready to leave the headquarters map. We will complete the preparations for an opening offensive and place responsibility for its execution with the command. Concentrating force can create a temporary opportunity, but the costs of mobilisation will not disappear with the first success.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_home_front: The campaign will demand recruits, public services and a population prepared to bear disruption. We will organise the home front and devote additional support to the people sustaining the war. Mobilisation can press the country into service, but coercion and sacrifice may also deepen divisions already present within Iraq.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_campaign_accounts: The promise of a decisive campaign must be tested against the men, supplies and money it consumes. We will bring the war's growing obligations into clearer view. If the fighting continues, attrition will reach well beyond the front and make an increasingly severe claim on the state's resources.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_secure_khuzestan: Holding Khuzestan requires a functioning rear as well as troops on the approaches. We will coordinate security, roads and public administration to give our position greater permanence. Control of a valuable province can strengthen Iraq, but maintaining that control will impose substantial new duties on the government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_long_war: The first campaign has not brought a decision, and Iran remains in the field. Baghdad must prepare to carry the struggle beyond its opening expectations. Another season of fighting will depend on reserves and resources that could otherwise sustain the country's development at home.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_oil_rehabilitation: Khuzestan's petroleum wealth will remain a distant prize while damaged connections and neglected facilities hinder its use. We will restore infrastructure and organise the administration supporting oil exports. Turning territorial gains into revenue requires sustained work and a substantial apparatus beyond the army's immediate needs.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_civil_administration: Military control cannot settle the ordinary affairs of a province indefinitely. We will recruit civilian officials and establish an administration capable of dealing with local records, services and public responsibilities. The new authorities will add to Baghdad's burdens long before they can command dependable local confidence.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_war_of_reserves: A prolonged struggle against Iran requires formations that can be replenished and held together after repeated losses. We will deepen the reserves and strengthen the organisation of the army. More men under arms will mean a heavier payroll and fewer specialists available for civilian and scientific work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_another_offensive: A new offensive offers the chance to break a costly stalemate, but it must rest on renewed preparation rather than the memory of the opening attack. We will assemble the supplies and resources required for another blow. Every fresh attempt will ask the country to carry another period of exceptional expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_regional_power: Possession of Khuzestan after a settlement would transform Iraq's position at the head of the Gulf. We will use that success to press a stronger regional role and consolidate the interests it has created. Greater influence brings wider commitments, and holding the prize will continue to demand capable government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_no_easy_exit: The longer the war continues, the more difficult it becomes to abandon its promised rewards. We will intensify military production and commit the resources needed to keep fighting. The additional strength will be drawn from civilian consumption, a strained military payroll and a public asked to endure still more sacrifice.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_provincial_settlement: A durable peace leaves Baghdad with the political task that conquest could only begin. We will establish a provincial settlement for Khuzestan and determine how its institutions relate to the Iraqi state. The negotiations and administration involved will demand attention that cannot simply be commanded into existence.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_equal_citizenship: A lasting Iraqi province needs residents who can expect a place in its institutions. We will provide equal citizenship, access to services and room for Arabic and Persian in provincial administration. A broader settlement may build confidence, but it requires a substantial commitment to administration and social provision.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_central_administration: Baghdad can seek permanence through a common chain of appointments and direct control over provincial affairs. We will bring Khuzestan under a more uniform state administration and limit the room for competing authorities. The approach is less demanding than wider local participation, but may deepen resentment toward rule from the capital.
COLDWAR_IRQ_iran_core_khuzestan: The claim to Khuzestan can become a lasting part of Iraq only after authority is sustained and ordinary institutions take root. We will complete the province's incorporation once security, infrastructure and public cooperation provide a firmer foundation. The ambition is to leave a functioning Iraqi province where there was once a contested conquest.
